MMA 28.3.113 (with a separate article on its mirror hieratic in the same volume); Hagen the rest.

exact_quotes: Summary (p. 214): 'Excavations at the mortuary temple of Thutmose III have revealed papyrus fragments that were produced for, and then burnt during, the ritual known as ‘Overthrowing Apophis’ (sxr aApp), through which the arch-enemy of the sun god Re was cursed.' The summary then refers to 'a 3rd Century BC papyrus (P. Bremner-Rhind = BM EA 10188)'.

Section 1 (p. 216): the three groups of fragments 'were discovered in a stratigraphic layer filled with ceramic remains' and 'the papyrus fragments analyzed in this study were found within a garbage dump context, surrounded by ceramic remains that tentatively suggest a date range from the mid- to late 18th Dynasty until the early 19th Dynasty'.
Section 2 (p. 216): P. Bremner-Rhind is 'a well-preserved and quite carefully copied hieratic manuscript from the late 4th Century BC, known as the Book of Overthrowing Apophis'.

Section 3 (p. 218): 'In total these amount to around 40 individual pieces, many of which are so fragmentary as to be difficult to identity in terms of type'. Both types are 'made from ‘new’ papyrus (i. e. not palimpsest), inscribed on one side only, using exclusively red ink'.

Section 3 (p. 218), grid lines: 'several examples of both types display characteristic red lines that delineate squares into which the drawings and the text have been inserted. The implication of this is that they were mass produced on an original sheet of papyrus that contained many such squares drawn up next to each other in a table format, and they were later cut up into individual sections'.
Section 3 (p. 218), size: the individual sections 'would have been c. 3–4 × 2–3 cm, similar to the squares drawn on the MMA piece'.
Section 3 (pp. 220-221): 'there can be no doubt that the fragments represent the material remains of that ritual.'

Section 5 (p. 224), burning and piercing: 'The burning is perhaps the most striking, and in some cases only tiny remains are left untouched by the fire, with carbonised edges. Some of the fragments also have holes which may be related to the ritual action of stabbing (Hw) with a knife (ds) or a spear (mabA), as their appearance is somewhat unusual for insect damage, for example'. Footnote 56: 'That the holes are a result of the ritual treatment was first suggested by Carina Kühne-Wespi.'

Section 6 (p. 226), counts and minimum performances: 'The total number of fragments that belong to Type I and Type II are roughly the same (twelve feature Apophis, while fourteen feature the Children of the Rebel), while the remaining sixteen or so fragments are in a state of preservation that makes the specific identification of type difficult. With a total of around 40 individual fragments, this suggests that the ritual was carried out, at a minimum, at twenty separate occasions, if each occasion featured a single example of both types—not necessarily enough to confirm it as a daily occurrence in this temple (see further below), but in our view a number that still suggests a certain regularity.'

Section 6 (p. 226), hedge: 'It is also possible that individual ritual events involved more than a single example of each of the two types of fragments, in which case the number of fragments is less indicative of frequency. In any case this would only provide a lower limit'.

Section 6 (p. 226), deposition: 'This would indicate that their original deposition was on many separate occasions ... it seems likely that after the execration ritual, which was presumably enacted somewhere inside the temple itself, they were swept up and carried outside for disposal.'

Section 6 (p. 228): 'The number of burnt fragments from the temple of Thutmose III confirms that the ritual was carried out repeatedly, but precisely on which days and at what time is impossible to say.'
Section 6, footnote 76 (p. 227), citing Müller-Roth 2008 on the nightly battles: 'Die ultimative Vernichtung ist unmöglich' ('ultimate annihilation is impossible').
Section 6 (p. 230): P. Bremner-Rhind's owner Nesmin 'somehow acquired the roll in the year mentioned in the ‘colophon’, around 305 BC'; and (p. 235) 'P. Bremner-Rhind itself (c. 305 BC)'.
Section 6 (p. 233), use outside temples: 'To what extent the ritual would have been accessible to, and performed by, people outside temples is more difficult to pin down'.
Section 6 (p. 235): 'The 18th Dynasty fragments from the temple of Thutmose III now provide the earliest direct evidence for these rituals found so far.'

Section 7 (p. 236), Decree for Amenhotep son of Hapu: those who take resources from his memorial temple are warned that the king's uraeus 'will spit fire (bS tkA) on their foreheads, will blacken their flesh, and eat their limbs, so that they become like Apophis on the morning of the New Year Festival' (citing Varille 1968, 8). The authors add: 'To an Egyptian audience this would not have been an obscure religious allusion to a myth, but a concrete reference to a well-known curse ritual that was strongly associated with the beginning of the year.'

Section 7 (p. 236): 'How well-known it was is not easy to say, but it may not be an exaggeration to suggest that it was probably not far behind such famous rituals as The Opening of the Mouth Ritual, The Daily Temple Ritual, and The Daily Cult Ritual.'
date_and_recency: Published online 5 November 2026 (print issue dated 3 November 2026 per Crossref). Material: the Thutmose III temple fragments are dated by associated pottery to the mid/late 18th Dynasty to early 19th Dynasty (the article calls them '18th Dynasty fragments', i.e. c. 14th century BC; press coverage rounds this to '3,400 years old'). P. MMA 28.3.113 is tentatively 26th Dynasty (Gardiner's palaeographic opinion on the museum tomb card; the Met dates it 25th-26th Dynasty). P. Bremner-Rhind is dated late 4th century BC, owner's colophon c. 305 BC (the article summary alone says 3rd century BC). Fragments found between 2014 and 2025.
key_claims: Charred papyrus fragments from the rubbish dump outside the north enclosure wall of Thutmose III's Temple of Millions of Years at Thebes are the material remains of the 'Overthrowing Apophis' curse ritual, and are the earliest direct evidence for it found so far.

Two types: Type I shows a single serpent, head turned downwards, cut by three knives, captioned 'Apophis who is the Roarer, who is the Terrifying-of-face'; Type II shows three serpent-like beings with non-serpent (possibly human) heads, captioned 'Children of the Rebel'. Both on new (non-palimpsest) papyrus, one side only, red ink only.

Red grid lines show they were mass produced in squares on larger sheets and then cut up; P. MMA 28.3.113, a later uncut sheet from Deir el-Bahri Tomb MMA 801 (with mirror-written hieratic on the recto), shows what such a sheet looked like. Small differences in hand and iconography mean the fragments came from more than one sheet and more than one scribe.

The fragments match the instructions in P. Bremner-Rhind closely (new papyrus, red ink, serpent with head down, the two epithets), and Bremner-Rhind 23.12 explicitly pairs 'the Roarer and the Terrifying-of-Face' when Apophis is put on the fire.
Burning (carbonised edges) and holes possibly from stabbing match the ritual's spells for spitting, trampling, spearing, binding, stabbing and setting fire.

About 40 fragments imply a minimum of twenty separate performances if each used one of each type: not enough to prove a daily rite, but suggesting regularity; a lower limit only, because the ritual was designed to destroy its own evidence.
Because the materials were burnt, physical survival is rare; clay execration figures are probably overrepresented in the record.
Mass-produced papyri suggest the wax figures were also made quickly, perhaps with stamps (though all known stamps are first millennium BC).

In temples, the Roman-period Book of the Temple assigns the ritual to the 'scribe of the god's book' (who likely drew and wrote the papyri) and the 'scorpion charmer' (who recited the Book of Overthrowing Apophis).

Bremner-Rhind lists times for the ritual (sunrise, midday, sunset, sixth hour of night, eighth hour of day, festivals) but also 'every hour of the day and night' and 'every day'; its claim that it was done at Karnak 'in the course of each day' may be literal or a device to lend authority.

Use outside temples is harder to establish; the text envisages private use against personal enemies, for protection and promotion, against storms and bad weather, and there are hints of therapeutic use against venom.

The Decree for Amenhotep son of Hapu's threat that offenders will 'become like Apophis on the morning of the New Year Festival' refers to a well-known curse ritual tied to the start of the year; the authors suggest the ritual's fame was probably not far behind the Opening of the Mouth and the Daily Temple Ritual.

dating_and_context: Found in the temple's rubbish dump north of (outside) the enclosure wall of Thutmose III's Temple of Millions of Years, near the side exit (grid 950 N5) that priests used to dispose of rubbish (Fig. 1 caption), in the eastern sector of the dump. Dated by context, not by the papyri themselves: the fragments lay in 'a stratigraphic layer filled with ceramic remains', and Bettina Bader's study of the dump pottery (many complete BB jars, types B and C; blue-painted vessels; bread moulds) 'tentatively suggest[s] a date range from the mid- to late 18th Dynasty until the early 19th Dynasty' (Bader and Seco Álvarez 2016). Pottery collection was selective (complete or at least 75% complete pieces, new types, painted wares) except in a 2015 test trench where everything was collected. No radiocarbon or palaeographic dating of the temple fragments is reported. Several grids yielded both types, which the authors read as deposition on many separate occasions after the ritual was performed, presumably inside the temple, and the debris swept out. P. MMA 28.3.113 comes from Tomb MMA 801 at Deir el-Bahri (Met excavations 1921–22), near an embalmers' cache; dated only by Gardiner's palaeographic guess of 26th Dynasty, which the authors accept with caution.
what_it_says_about_apophis: Apophis is the great serpent and main enemy of the sun god Re during his perilous night journey through the underworld, after which Re rises and brings a new day; the battle is 'recurring' and a key concern of New Kingdom netherworld books (Amduat 7th hour: 'one slaughters Apophis in the Netherworld'). The Amduat says the magic used to repel Apophis 'is done in the secrecy of the Netherworld, and likewise it is done on earth', which the authors say has 'some truth in it' given the ritual. Footnote 76 notes the episodic, recurring nature of the nightly battles and quotes Müller-Roth's conclusion that 'Die ultimative Vernichtung ist unmöglich' (ultimate annihilation is impossible), reiterated by Backes 2025. Epithets used: 'the Roarer' (hmhm.ty) and 'the Terrifying-of-face' (nHA-Hr); 'Children of the Rebel' are a manifestation of Apophis or beings in their own right. The ritual's times track solar events and the hours of the main mythical battles. Mythic conflict is mirrored on earth in the king's struggle against his enemies, and the text also blames Apophis for storms and bad weather.
ritual_practice: Per P. Bremner-Rhind and the fragments: drawings of Apophis and the Children of the Rebel in red ink on new papyrus, captioned with names; wax figures of Apophis (red wax, name inscribed in red ink), sometimes bound and placed in a container; enemies of the king (with names of parents and children) drawn and modelled in wax. Spells accompany spitting on Apophis, trampling with the left foot, spearing, binding, stabbing with a knife and setting fire to him, using bryony (xAs) kindling and 'the fire in the furnace of the coppersmiths'. The temple fragments show charring and holes that may be from stabbing. Papyri were mass produced in gridded sheets and cut into squares; wax figures were perhaps stamped. Performed presumably inside the temple, then the debris swept out to the dump. Personnel (from the Roman-period Book of the Temple): the 'scribe of the god's book' made the written objects; the 'scorpion charmer' recited the Book of Overthrowing Apophis; lector priests also feature. The officiant speaks as Pharaoh. Later temple inscriptions (Esna, Medamud, Kom Ombo, Edfu) link recitations to specific festivals; Esna adds four red goats and throwing the remains into water. Possible funerary/embalming use (MMA papyrus findspot; Apis embalming list), and possible private and therapeutic use.
prescribed_vs_attested_frequency: Prescribed: P. Bremner-Rhind says the ritual was done at Karnak 'in the course of each day' and lists sunrise, midday, sunset, the sixth hour of the night, the eighth hour of the day, the new-moon, monthly, sixth-day and fifteenth-day festivals, and 'every hour of the day and night' and 'every day'; one instruction says to put Apophis on the fire 'every day' (28.16); BD 15A speaks of performing it 'every day'; storms call for doing it 'very often'. The authors caution that such meta-textual statements tend to hyperbole and may lend authority rather than describe practice. Attested: about 40 fragments (12 Apophis, 14 Children of the Rebel, ~16 unassigned) imply at least 20 performances if each used one of each type, 'not necessarily enough to confirm it as a daily occurrence in this temple' but suggesting 'a certain regularity'; if performances used more than one of each, the count says less about frequency; and it is only a lower limit because most burnt papyri would not survive or be recognised. The authors conclude it was 'carried out repeatedly, but precisely on which days and at what time is impossible to say'. Separately, the Amenhotep son of Hapu decree ties it to the New Year Festival morning.
relevance_to_angle: Strongly supportive. The myth frames Apophis as a recurring enemy who is never finally destroyed (the article footnotes Müller-Roth: ultimate annihilation is impossible), and the ritual's prescription for every day, every hour and recurring festivals reflects routine upkeep rather than a single victory. The archaeology shows mass-produced, disposable, gridded papyrus squares made in batches by temple scribes and burnt over and over (at least twenty occasions), then swept out with the temple rubbish: maintenance as routine institutional work. The storm passage ('do this very often ... to prevent bad weather') is explicitly preventative. Complications: the authors refuse to confirm daily performance; minimum counts depend on an assumption (one of each type per rite); the 'each day' and 'every hour' claims may be authority-lending hyperbole; and the Amenhotep son of Hapu decree links the ritual especially to the New Year, suggesting calendar peaks as well as routine.
limitations_stated: (1) Pottery dating 'tentatively' suggests mid/late 18th to early 19th Dynasty. (2) Minimum of twenty occasions holds only 'if each occasion featured a single example of both types'; 'not necessarily enough to confirm it as a daily occurrence'; multiple examples per event would make the count 'less indicative of frequency'; 'this would only provide a lower limit'. (3) About 16 fragments too damaged to type; only the best preserved published here, the full series reserved for a final publication; 2025 groups not yet conserved or fully studied. (4) Holes 'may be related' to stabbing, judged unusual for insect damage, not proven. (5) Original square size cannot be established precisely because no fragment preserves both sides. (6) Findspots say little beyond multiple depositions; where and when the ritual was done is inferred. (7) Meta-textual claims in Bremner-Rhind (daily use at Karnak, secrecy of the House of Life) may be hyperbole or authority-lending; 'caution must be exercised'. (8) Palaeographic dating of P. MMA 28.3.113 'must be rather uncertain'. (9) Funerary use 'conceivable' but evidence not 'conclusive in any sense'. (10) Use outside temples 'more difficult to pin down'; evidence for private use is limited. (11) Stamps for wax figures are attested only in the first millennium BC; their use in the second millennium is 'unknown'. (12) The supporting sources for the ritual's status are 'suggestive rather than conclusive when analysed individually'. (13) How well known the ritual was 'is not easy to say'.
source_discrepancies: (1) P. Bremner-Rhind date: the article's own summary says '3rd Century BC', while the body says 'late 4th Century BC' and gives the owner's colophon as 'around 305 BC' / 'c. 305 BC'; the body is more specific (c. 305 BC falls at the very end of the 4th century). Other sources should be checked against c. 305 BC. (2) Fragment count: 'around 40' total versus 12 + 14 + 'sixteen or so' = about 42; press reports repeating '40' and the 12/14/16 split are consistent with the paper. (3) Footnote 68 says single-name curse figures were widely used 'also in the 2nd Millennium CE, not just in the 1st Millennium CE', evidently a slip for BCE given the 18th Dynasty date. (4) Press coverage (e.g. PopSci) reportedly named the journal differently ('Journal of the Egyptian Language and Antiquities'); the paper and Crossref give ZÄS. (5) Ink: the paper says exclusively red ink on both types; no conflict seen. (6) Press '3,400 years old' is a rounding of the 18th Dynasty pottery date; the paper itself gives no year count. (7) The paper says the ritual was 'presumably enacted somewhere inside the temple itself'; press phrasing that priests performed it in the temple overstates certainty slightly. (8) Footnote 18 says the enemies are called Snty 'five times' but lists six references (24.1, 27.22, 28.12, 29.10, 30.7, 30.20).
